title: Portrait of a Lady

altText: A very small painted portrait of a woman, shown in a close-up view. It is painted in delicate watercolor on a thin piece of ivory.

context: A portrait miniature painted by the American artist Henry Inman around 1825 in watercolor on ivory. It measures about 8.6 by 6 centimeters (3 3/8 by 2 3/8 inches), small enough to hold in one hand.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny painting of a woman. It is so small you can hold it in your hand. The artist used watery paint on a thin piece of ivory. Look at her face. What do you think she is feeling?
descriptions.g12: This painting of a woman is very small. It is about the size of a playing card, or smaller. Henry Inman painted it with watercolor on a thin sheet of ivory, around 1825. Look at her face and the soft colors. What do you think she wants us to know about her?
descriptions.g35: Henry Inman painted this portrait around 1825. It is a miniature, a tiny painting made to be held and looked at up close. He used watercolor on a thin piece of ivory, which gives the skin a soft glow. The painting is only about 8.6 centimeters tall. What details of her face and her clothing would an artist need to paint very carefully?
descriptions.g68: Portrait miniatures were small, personal paintings, often kept in a pocket, worn as jewelry, or given to family and friends. Henry Inman painted this one in watercolor on ivory around 1825, a surface that gives skin tones a luminous, soft quality. At about 8.6 centimeters tall, every brushstroke needs to be tiny and controlled. How does the small size make a portrait feel more personal?
descriptions.g910: In this miniature of about 1825, Henry Inman uses watercolor on ivory, a combination that lets thin, transparent color glow because the pale surface reflects light back through the paint. The small format, about 8.6 by 6 centimeters, demands precise handling and invites intimate, close looking. The record does not name the sitter, so the portrait is both an individual likeness and an anonymous face. Consider what a small portrait offers that a large one cannot.
descriptions.g1112: Inman's miniature of about 1825 belongs to a tradition of small portraits made for private exchange, remembrance, and display. Watercolor on ivory produces luminous, delicate flesh tones, but it also constrains how much can be shown at this scale. The Met titles the work Portrait of a Lady and does not identify the sitter in the title, which shifts attention from biography to craft and convention. How does an unnamed portrait invite us to think about likeness, intimacy, and the limits of what a face can tell us?

teacherNote.context: A portrait miniature by the American painter Henry Inman, about 1825, in watercolor on ivory and about 8.6 cm tall. The sitter is not named in the title, so discussion can focus on technique, scale, and the purpose of keepsake portraits. Ivory is a sensitive material today; it was a common support for miniatures in this period.
directions: Ask students to paint or draw a portrait of a classmate on a card the size of a deck of cards and discuss what changes at small scale.
Discuss why people keep tiny images of loved ones and how photography changed that tradition.
Compare this miniature with a large portrait in the archive and discuss intimacy versus display.
